food.text: Herodotus's Histories, written in the 5th century BC, describes the Scythians preparing mare's milk, the drink known today as kumis or airag. According to Herodotus, the Scythians blinded all their slaves to use them in this work. They thrust tubes made of bone up the vulva of the mare and blew into them with their mouths, because they said air in the animal's veins forced the udder down. The milk was then poured into deep wooden casks, with the blind slaves placed around them, and stirred round.

By around 1200 BCE, people across the Eastern Eurasian Steppe, in what is now Mongolia, were already drinking horse milk, as shown by analysis of dental plaque. This shift came alongside the rise of mobile pastoralism and the earliest bridling and riding of horses.

After the Han dynasty expanded into Central Asia around 114 BCE, Silk Road traders sent tea, dyes, perfumes and porcelain westward out of China. Horses, camels, honey and wine moved the other way, carried eastward toward Central Asia from the Mediterranean along the same routes.

This ancient drink stayed only mildly alcoholic, between 0.7 and 2.5 percent, because mare's milk is rich in sugars that ferment directly. That places kumis, technically, closer to wine than to the grain-based beer it resembles in taste and use.

Kumis, the fermented mare's-milk drink, could be strengthened through freeze distillation, a technique Central Asian nomads are reported to have used. This let steppe peoples boost its naturally mild alcohol content.
Kumis could also be made into a stronger, distilled drink called arkhi. This was another way Central Asian nomads used the same mare's-milk fermenting tradition to get a stronger beverage.

art.text: From the late second millennium BC, herders migrating across the grasslands of Central Asia made 'animal style' art. It shows their zoomorphic mythologies and shamanic traditions, and also how easily they worked the symbols of settled societies into their own artworks.

The artistic remains of Central Asia combine many influences, including Scythian art, Greco-Buddhist art and Serindian art. The region was a crossroads of cultural exchange and the hub of the Silk Road, the complex system of trade routes stretching from China to the Mediterranean.

The Greco-Bactrians ruled southern Central Asia from the 3rd to the 2nd century BC, with their capital at Ai-Khanoum. Excavations show a Greek city of 1.5 square kilometers with a Classical theater, temples and a gymnasium measuring 100 by 100 meters, one of the largest of Antiquity.

Ai-Khanoum had a huge palace in Greco-Bactrian architecture, somehow reminiscent of formal Persian palatial architecture. Some structures in the city were perfectly Hellenistic while others integrated elements of Persian architecture, showing a high Hellenistic culture combined with Eastern influences.

Contacts with nomadic peoples on China's western and northwestern borders from the 8th century BC brought Central Asian influence into China. The Chinese adopted the Scythian-style animal art of the steppes, especially rectangular belt-plaques of gold or bronze, and made their own versions in jade and steatite.

Under the Indo-Greeks, and especially later under the Kushan Empire, Greco-Buddhist art flourished in Gandhara and even spread to Central Asia, affecting the art of the Tarim Basin. This art was a blend of Ancient Greek art and Buddhism.

Among the finds at Ai-Khanoum was a mosaic representing the Macedonian sun, acanthus leaves and various animals such as crabs and dolphins. Archaeologists also found numerous remains of Classical Corinthian columns, and many artifacts date to the 2nd century BC.

The Kushans were a nomadic people who started migrating from the Tarim Basin in Central Asia from around 170 BC. After conquering lands once inhabited by Greco-Bactrians and Indo-Greeks, their empire in northwestern India adopted Greco-Buddhist art.

Ai-Khanoum was one of the major cities when the Greek kings started to occupy parts of India, from 200 to 145 BC. The article says it flourished until nomadic invaders destroyed it in 145 BC. It seems the city was never rebuilt, and its destruction came about the time of the death of king Eucratides around 145 BC.

Murals in the Tarim Basin city of Dunhuang describe the ambassador Zhang Qian traveling as far as Bactria around 130 BC. They also show Emperor Wu worshipping Buddhist statues described as golden men brought in 120 BC, which suggests Buddha statues already existed in the 2nd century BC.

war.text: The steppe nomads' way of life suited warfare well. Their horse archers used devastating techniques, and the steppe riders became some of the most militarily potent people in the world. Relations between these nomads and the settled peoples around Central Asia were marked by conflict, and the nomads often carried out raids because they had few goods of interest to sedentary people. Settled states and cities were forced to pay them tribute or face annihilation.
During the 1st millennium BCE, powers such as the Scythians and the Xiongnus emerged in North Asia. They often clashed with their Persian and Chinese neighbors to the south.

Alexander the Great pushed deep into Central Asia and founded Alexandria Eschate, meaning "Alexandria the Furthest", in 329 BC. It stood in what is now Tajikistan. His conquests spread Hellenistic civilisation all the way to this city, and he founded cities and took control of the trading centres along the way.
The Xiongnu Empire, which lasted from 209 BC to 93 AD, may be seen as the first Central Asian empire. It set an example for the later Göktürk and Mongol empires.

In the 2nd and 1st millennia BC, powerful states on the southern edge of Central Asia launched several attempts to conquer the steppe peoples. They met with only mixed success. The Median Empire and the Achaemenid Empire both did rule parts of Central Asia.

Steppe tribes could periodically unite into a single military force and launch campaigns of conquest, especially into more "civilized" areas. The Huns' invasion of Europe is one example of such a tribal coalition. When large numbers of nomads acted in unison they could be devastating, and the scattered city states and kingdoms near them had to pay tribute or face annihilation.

After Alexander the Great died in 323 BC, his Central Asian territory fell to the Seleucid Empire during the Wars of the Diadochi. Then in 250 BC, the Central Asian portion, Bactria, seceded as the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom.

literature.text: The Kushan Empire, which the article dates from 30 AD to 375 AD, adopted the Greek alphabet for writing the Bactrian language. It also took over Greco-Buddhist art forms and coinage from the earlier Hellenistic kingdoms of Central Asia.

Classical Indian literature records peoples such as the Shakas, Yavanas, Kambojas, Pahlavas and Paradas as arriving in India as invaders. According to the article, they were ultimately assimilated into Indian society as Kshatriyas.
literature.source_title: Central Asians in ancient Indian literature

literature.text: The Chinese monk Zhu Shixing, who died after 282, reported that by the 3rd century CE some Mahāyāna texts were known in Khotan. This shows Buddhist writings were already circulating along the Silk Road kingdoms of Central Asia.

The Puranas describe the Haihaya Yadavas allying with four other groups; the invaders were eventually defeated and assimilated into the local community under castes ranging from Kshatriyas to Shudras. Alberuni, referring to this description, said the "five hordes" belonged to his own people, meaning Central Asia. The Haihaya Yadavas are the first known invaders in the recorded history of the sub-continent.
literature.source_title: Central Asians in ancient Indian literature

literature.text: An inscription in the Kharoṣṭhī script was found at Endere, written around the middle of the 3rd century CE. It describes the king of Shanshan as one who has "set forth in the Great Vehicle". The king was probably Aṃgoka, and Richard Salomon sees Mahāyāna as enjoying royal patronage there.

The Chinese author Ma-twan-lin wrote that the names of the early Sakas in India show a mixture of Scythian, Parthian and Iranian elements. He added that the Scythians soon adapted to their new surroundings and began to adopt Indian names and religious beliefs.
literature.source_title: Central Asians in ancient Indian literature

science.text: The Issyk kurgan in south-eastern Kazakhstan, dated to the 4th or 3rd century BC, held more than 4,000 gold items along with an iron sword, a dagger and a bronze mirror. These finds reveal the skilled metalworking of the Saka people who buried their dead there.

Mummified remains from Pazyryk culture kurgans in the Altai Mountains of Siberia and Mongolia, dated to about 400 to 200 BCE, still bear tattoos of real and fantastical animals in the Scytho-Siberian Animal Style. These tattoos are believed to have encoded information about social status, gender and religious beliefs. Post-mortem surgical cuts were made through the tattooed skin of some bodies, which suggests that the tattoos' ritual function ended with the bearer's death.

In 36 BCE, at a battle near Sogdiana, Han Chinese troops met Roman legionaries who had probably been captured or recruited as mercenaries by the Xiongnu. The Han expedition apparently defeated them. According to R. Ernest Dupuy and Trevor N. Dupuy, the margin of Chinese victory appears to have been their crossbows, whose bolts and darts seem easily to have penetrated Roman shields and armour. It has been suggested that the Chinese crossbow reached the Roman world on such occasions, though the Greek gastraphetes offers an alternative origin.

The Xiongnu Empire, which lasted from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE, grew out of hybrid Saka cultures. It combined Saka ancestries with Ulaanzuukh and Slab Grave ancestries, and later added Sarmatian and Han ancestry. High status Xiongnu individuals had less genetic diversity than low status ones.

At Issyk, gold ornaments covered the clothing, headdress and shoes of the young occupant later known as the Golden Man, and even the handle of a whip found beside the body was wrapped in a spiral ribbon of gold. Such craftsmanship suggests the Saka nobility could commission fine goldsmithing.

Seven tattooed individuals have been recovered from four kurgan sites: Pazyryk, Ak-Alakha 3 and Verkh-Kaldzhin 2 in Russia, and Olon-Kurin-Gol 10 in Mongolia. Permafrost preserved their skin and soft tissue, but many tattoos had nearly or completely vanished as the skin darkened and the bodies decomposed after excavation. The tattoos were made by pricking the skin with multi-point and single-point tools and rubbing in a colorant, likely soot from burned vegetation, sometimes over several sessions.

The tattooing tradition seen among the Pazyryk continued into later centuries, as shown by a mummy from the Tashtyk culture site of Oglakhty in Khakassia. This later find shows the same body-art practice persisting among later Iron Age peoples of Siberia.

A likely Xiongnu chanyu, identified by his prestigious tomb, was found to have about 39.3% Slab Grave ancestry, 51.9% Han ancestry and 8.8% Saka ancestry. He had a similar profile to a high status woman in the western frontiers. The Xiongnu ruling class thus blended eastern Eurasian and Han ancestry.

politics.text: Under Kanishka, the Kushan emperor, forces marched north from the Indian subcontinent across Kashmir's Karokam Mountains into Bactria. They captured Kabul, Bagram and Peshawar, then pushed on to Sogdiana, Fergana and East Turkestan. The campaign gave the Kushans control over key Silk Road routes across Central Asia.

Emperor Wu of Han sent Zhang Qian to the Western Regions in 115 BC to seek military alliances against the Xiongnu. He approached Central Asian states such as the Wusun. He returned without winning the alliances, but he brought back valuable knowledge about the region.

By the 2nd and 3rd centuries CE, the Kangju kingdom in Transoxiana minted its own coinage, styled similarly to the currency of Khwarezm. This independent coinage shows Kangju's standing as a regional power even as it kept sending embassies to the Han court.

Zhang Qian told Emperor Wu of the large, powerful horses of Ferghana, called "heavenly horses". The emperor thought they were important for fighting the Xiongnu. When the Dayuan kingdom refused to supply them and executed a Han envoy, war followed, and the Han forces brought Dayuan into submission in 101 BC.

Kanishka converted to Buddhism and promoted it at the state level. His conquest of Greater Bactria and the Silk Road routes strengthened the Kushan economy and fostered cultural syncretism. Zoroastrian, Hindu Shaivite and Greco-Roman themes were folded into the dominant Buddhist culture.

The Xiongnu king Modu Chanyu defeated the Donghu confederation, leaving the Xianbei and Wuhuan as its main remnants. In 49 CE the Xianbei ruler Bianhe raided and defeated the Xiongnu, killing 2000, after receiving generous gifts from Emperor Guangwu of Han. The Xianbei reached their peak under Tanshihuai, who reigned 156 to 181.

The Han dynasty established the Protectorate of the Western Regions in 60 BC to administer what is now Xinjiang. Its Protector General was stationed at Wulei, west of Karasahr. After the Western Han ended in 9 AD, China lost authority there until the Eastern Han restored it in 94 AD.

According to the Hou Hanshu, a Kushan army of 70,000 troops met the Han general Ban Chao near Khotan in 90 CE. Despite Ban Chao's scorched-earth strategy, the large force showed that the Kushans could challenge Han power in the Tarim Basin. The Han had seen the Kushans as a threat to their western flank.

According to Chinese chronicles, the Kushans requested a Han princess and were denied. In retaliation they marched on the general Ban Chao in AD 90 with a force of 70,000, but were defeated by the smaller Chinese force. The Yuezhi then retreated and paid tribute to the Chinese Empire.

philosophy.text: Buddhism dominated pre-Islamic Central Asia, mostly in Mahayana forms, and was especially prevalent along the Silk Road. Its history there is closely tied to the Silk Road transmission of Buddhism during the first millennium of the common era.

Buddhism in Central Asia began with a blend of Western Classical Greek philosophy and Indian Buddhism. This happened in the Hellenistic successor kingdoms to Alexander the Great's empire: the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom (250 BCE to 125 BCE) and the Indo-Greek Kingdom (180 BCE to 10 CE).

Tengrism is a belief system that originated in the Eurasian steppes. It is based on shamanism and animism and is commonly centered on the sky god Tengri. According to some scholars, its followers saw the purpose of life as living in harmony with the universe.

The Iranian peoples emerged as a separate branch of the Indo-Iranians in the 2nd millennium BC, and came to dominate the Eurasian Steppe and the Persian Plateau. Their religion shares many similarities with the Vedic religion of India, though little written evidence of it survives.

The later Kushan empire adopted the Greek alphabet for the Bactrian language, along with Greco-Buddhist art forms and coinage. It also took over the Greco-Buddhist religion of the earlier Hellenistic kingdoms.

At the start of the Kushan dynasty around 30 AD, many religious systems coexisted in Central Asia. They included the cult of Anahit, which originated in Armenia, Zoroastrianism, and the Greek pantheon with gods such as Zeus and Helios.

Tengrism was the prevailing religion of several steppe peoples, including the Hun, Xianbei, Xiongnu and Yeniseian peoples. This shows how widely the sky-god tradition was shared across the Eurasian steppes.

Tengrism differed from Siberian shamanism because it was a more organized religion. It was practiced by a succession of pastoral, semi-sedentary khanates and empires beginning with the Xiongnu empire, founded in 209 BC, not by small bands of hunter-gatherers like the Paleosiberians.

Tengrism was a popular religion in ancient Central Asia and Siberia, a form of animism. The central act in the relationship between humans and nature was the worship of the Blue Mighty Eternal Heaven, also called the Blue Sky.

Among the Zoroastrian cults widespread in Central Asia at the start of the Kushan dynasty were those of Mithra, Ormuzd and Verethragna. The cult of Siyâvash was especially popular in Khorezm and Sogd.

culture.text: The Pazyryk culture was an Iron Age nomadic culture of the 6th to 3rd centuries BC. It is known from artifacts and mummified humans found in the Siberian permafrost, in the Altai Mountains, Kazakhstan and Mongolia. The dead were buried in long barrows, or kurgans.
No settlements have been found that go with the Pazyryk burials. This suggests that the Pazyryk lived a purely nomadic lifestyle, leaving their mark mainly in kurgan cemeteries.

During the 1st millennium BC, Iranian-speaking peoples including the Saka (Scythians), Sarmatians and Alans dominated the old Andronovo horizon. Iranian place-names spread across that vast area are among the evidence linking it to the Indo-Iranians.

The Pazyryk burials of the Ukok Plateau contained many artifacts and human remains, including the Siberian Ice Princess. They point to a flourishing culture that benefited from the trade routes and caravans of merchants passing through the area.

Turkic and Mongolic languages share extensive similarities, and words passed between the peoples long before Genghis Khan. Extensive borrowing from Proto-Turkic into Proto-Mongolic happened from the first millennium BCE at the latest.

That same shift in Mongolia around 1200 BCE also brought the earliest evidence of horses being bridled and ridden on the steppe. It coincided too with the practice of burying horses in ritual mounds known as khirigsuurs.
The Pazyryk culture was preceded by the Arzhan culture of the 8th to 7th century BC, known as the Initial Scythian period. This places the Pazyryk in a longer line of Scythian-related steppe peoples.

According to the Discourses of the States, the Xianbei attended a meeting of Zhou subject-lords at Qiyang in the reign of King Cheng of Zhou (1042–1021 BCE). Because they were not vassals, they were only allowed to perform the fire ceremony under Chu supervision. Their chieftain was made joint guardian of the ritual torch alongside the Chu viscount Xiong Yi.

Turkic and Mongolic languages share deeper traits such as vowel harmony, no grammatical gender, extensive agglutination and very similar phonotactic rules. These suggest an even older period of prolonged contact between the two language families, before the Turkic people broke up around 500 BCE.

Other kurgan cemeteries associated with the Pazyryk culture include those of Bashadar, Tuekta, Ulandryk, Polosmak and Berel. Together with the Ukok Plateau burials, they mark the culture's presence across the Altai region.

During the Warring States period, the poem "The Great Summons" in the anthology Verses of Chu mentions small-waisted and long-necked Xianbei women. It is a rare glimpse of how the Xianbei were pictured by their southern neighbours.
